forces: Contralto and tenor soloists, mixed chorus, organ and orchestra
performers: Oralia Domínguez, contralto; Raymond Amade, tenor; J. J. Grunenwald, organ; Chorale Élisabeth Brasseur; Orchestre des Concerts Lamoureux; Igor Markevitch, conductor
intro: Tuba and solo cello share a low lament in Boulanger’s vast setting of Psalm 130, dedicated to her father’s memory. Igor Markevitch conducts, with Oralia Domínguez’s contralto carrying the long solo prayer at its centre.

cues.title: Tuba beside a solo cello
cues.text: The organ holds its low notes above a soft bass-drum roll and plucked strings. A tuba and a solo cello enter together, falling by a tone. Their line lies deep below the silent choir; muted horns join it.
cues.evidence: Durand full score (1925), plate D. & F. 10543, p. 1: Lent librement, organ, bass drum, pizzicato cellos and basses; tuba and solo cello from bar 3, muted horns later on the page. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/28/IMSLP393069-PMLP430943-N0856389_PDF_1_-1DM.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: B♭ minor, the key of the abyss
cues.text: Christopher Palmer calls B♭ minor, for Lili, “the key of the abyss, of mourning and despair”. Its gloom covers this psalm and her Musset setting Pour les funérailles d’un soldat. Gerald Larner adds that modal inflections make the introduction’s harmonies more oppressive still.
cues.evidence: Christopher Palmer, notes for Hyperion CDA66726 (1994): https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA66726. Gerald Larner, programme note on Psaume 130: https://geraldlarner.com/work/boulanger-psaume-130

cues.title: Violins climb out of the bass
cues.text: The prelude reaches the violins’ high notes. Both violin sections wind upwards through sharps and naturals, briefly playing alone. A little acceleration carries their runs over the top; Élargi broadens the descent.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 3–4, after figure 1: high first and second violins, Rubato, Poco accel. and Élargi.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Rome and the family home
cues.text: Boulanger begins the psalm in Rome in 1914 and completes its orchestration at Gargenville, the family home, in 1917. The dates and places stand together on the last page.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, p. 90, dated Rome–Gargenville 1914–1917. Helen Julia Minors’s preface (2011) identifies Gargenville as the family home and dates the completed orchestration to 1917. https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/1001.html

cues.title: The first human voices
cues.text: The choir enters quietly, all four parts singing the same narrow line in octaves. Boulanger writes sobre, mais intense — restrained, but intense. Bassoons and cellos climb underneath; the organ holds the bass.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, p. 11, figure 4: Tempo lent, pp sobre, mais intense, octave choral entry, rising bassoons and cellos, sustained organ pedal.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Chanting, then supplication
cues.text: On its first entry, Gerald Larner writes, the chorus “merely chants the words”. Only gradually, through a lyrical expansion on the holy names “Iahvé” and “Adonaï”, does it find melody for sustained supplication.
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner, programme note on Psaume 130: https://geraldlarner.com/work/boulanger-psaume-130

cues.title: For her father
cues.text: Above the title Boulanger writes ‘à la mémoire de mon cher Papa’ — to the memory of my dear Papa. Ernest Boulanger dies in 1900, when she is six. His daughter puts the dedication over the psalm’s first low instrumental notes.
cues.evidence: Lili Boulanger’s dedication on the first page of Psalm 130, completed in 1917, Durand full score (1925), p. 1. Ernest Boulanger’s death and Lili’s age are given in Helen Julia Minors’s preface (2011). https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/1001.html

cues.title: The record that changed Palmer’s life
cues.text: Christopher Palmer, then a student, first heard Lili Boulanger on “the classic Markevich record originally issued on the Everest label”: this one. He wrote to Nadia at once, and the music, he says, “effectively changed my life”. In the summer of 1967 he studied with her at Fontainebleau.
cues.evidence: Christopher Palmer, notes for Hyperion CDA66726 (1994): https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA66726

cues.title: A climax on “Adonaï”
cues.text: The quicker second section opens as the first did, with soft chanting, and builds to a broad climax on the “Adonaï” material. Then the chorus yields to the alto soloist, who brings a new melody in E♭ minor at a more relaxed tempo and in a more intimate texture.
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner, programme note on Psaume 130: https://geraldlarner.com/work/boulanger-psaume-130

cues.title: Contralto and cello together
cues.text: The choir falls silent as Oralia Domínguez begins the question about human sin. A solo cello joins her line. Clarinets repeat their rising figures, harps mark the pulse, and divided violins hold very soft chords above the voice.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 37–40, figure 12: contralto entry, solo cello, repeated clarinet and bass-clarinet figures, two harps and divided violins marked ppp.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A committee for musicians at war
cues.text: When war breaks out Lili is at the Villa Medici in Rome. She writes to fellow musicians to build a support network for those serving in the war, and with Nadia founds the Comité Franco-Américain du Conservatoire. Nadia wins the backing of American artists and diplomats.
cues.evidence: Library of Congress, “Lili Boulanger”, Women in French history research guide: https://guides.loc.gov/feminism-french-women-history/famous/lili-boulanger

cues.title: Who can stand?
cues.text: The chorus takes fright again, asking with growing insistency “Qui donc pourra tenir?” — who can stand? Its most emphatic asking, Gerald Larner writes, comes on a fortissimo augmentation of the trumpet call from the introduction.
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner, programme note on Psaume 130: https://geraldlarner.com/work/boulanger-psaume-130

cues.title: Bassoon, flute, viola, cello
cues.text: A solo bassoon begins the interlude, marked chanté, calme. Flute, viola and cello take their turns above running notes in the harps and organ. The string sections put on mutes; the solo viola and cello keep theirs off.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 54–56, Modéré and Rubato interlude: solo bassoon and flute, solo viola and cello, harp and organ semiquavers, selective string-muting instructions.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The turning point
cues.text: Gerald Larner calls the third section the turning point of the work. The tempo slows; over rippling arpeggios in harp and organ, a new woodwind melody passes to the alto, who sings “Mais la clémence est en toi”: but mercy is in you.
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner, programme note on Psaume 130, third section; the English of the sung line is our translation. https://geraldlarner.com/work/boulanger-psaume-130

cues.title: The conductor, Igor Markevitch
cues.text: Igor Markevitch was born in Kiev in 1912. At thirteen he went to Paris to study piano with Alfred Cortot; in his teens he studied with Nadia Boulanger and Paul Dukas. At seventeen he composed a work for Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes.
cues.evidence: Everest LPBR 6059 (1960), sleeve note on the conductor: https://archive.org/download/lp_du-fond-de-labime-psaume-24-psaume-129_lili-boulanger-igor-markevitch-orchestre-d/lp_du-fond-de-labime-psaume-24-psaume-129_lili-boulanger-igor-markevitch-orchestre-d_djvu.txt

cues.title: The tenor answers below
cues.text: Domínguez sings a new phrase, very softly; Raymond Amade’s tenor repeats it a fifth lower. Their lines overlap above rising flute figures and falling organ notes. The score asks for Sans lenteur — without dragging.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 70–73, figure 19: Sans lenteur, contralto and tenor canon with flute, harp and organ. The fifth-below imitation is also described in Helen Julia Minors’s preface (2011).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Major harmonies at last
cues.text: In the fourth section, where a tenor joins the alto, Gerald Larner hears Lili’s vision “at last” glimpse “the radiance of major harmonies”. The earlier sections stay weighed down by oppressive modal inflections.
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner, programme note on Psaume 130: https://geraldlarner.com/work/boulanger-psaume-130

cues.title: Never heard in her lifetime
cues.text: Lili never heard her finest scores played. Christopher Palmer lists Du fond de l’abîme among those unperformed in her lifetime and adds that when they were, “no changes were needed apart from a few modifications of dynamics”.
cues.evidence: Christopher Palmer, notes for Hyperion CDA66726 (1994): https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA66726

cues.title: The lower voices press on
cues.text: An Allegro breaks into the choir’s held chords. Tenors and basses begin the promise of redemption while clarinets, bassoons and lower strings race through detached figures. The upper strings remove their mutes, and the gathering orchestra accelerates.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 81–85, figure 22 onwards: Allegro, lower-voice entry, detached wind and string figures, removal of violin mutes and acceleration.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Back into the depths
cues.text: The rush gives way to Lent. Choir, brass and organ return to broad calls on God’s name, with the bass plunging below them. The closing prayer gradually sheds its instruments; after the voices stop, one last orchestral swell remains.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 86–90, figure 23 Lent, broad choral phrases and low bass writing; De plus en plus lent and Molto rit. on the final page, with the last instrumental swell after the choir’s release.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One side of an LP
cues.text: Everest puts this whole twenty-four-minute psalm on side one of LPBR 6059. The four shorter works fill side two.
cues.evidence: Track listing of the Everest LP, 1960: https://archive.org/details/lp_du-fond-de-labime-psaume-24-psaume-129_lili-boulanger-igor-markevitch-orchestre-d

cues.title: Without easy consolation
cues.text: Gerald Larner hears the work end “without the unambiguous consolation Lili was too honest to provide”, even after a last, liberated climax on “Iahvé, Adonaï” and an ethereal expression of hope.
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner, programme note on Psaume 130: https://geraldlarner.com/work/boulanger-psaume-130

transitions.title: The choir rises from the bass
transitions.to: A · The choir enters in octaves
transitions.how: The B♭ minor prelude slows, with trombones marked morendo. At figure 4, Tempo lent, the choir enters on repeated notes in octaves. A held organ bass remains beneath the voices while bassoons and cellos climb together. The bass drum rolls softly behind the first words.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 10–12, figure 4: Rit., morendo trombones, Tempo lent, quiet choir, organ pedal and rising bassoon/cello line.

transitions.title: A solo cello joins the singer
transitions.from: A · The choir enters in octaves
transitions.how: The chorus holds its final vowel as the metre changes to 3/2 at figure 12. The contralto enters over a solo cello, repeated clarinet figures and harp chords. Divided violins hold ppp above her; the organ’s low notes keep the slow pulse while the brass fall silent.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 36–38, figure 12: change to 3/2, contralto and solo cello, rising clarinets, harps, organ bass and divided ppp violins.

transitions.title: The bassoon begins alone
transitions.to: C · Bassoon, flute and solo strings
transitions.how: At Modéré the choir releases its last syllable and the brass chords die away. A solo bassoon begins above the organ’s held bass and running harp notes. Flute and solo viola follow; the remaining strings put on mutes as the accompaniment thins.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 53–56: Modéré, choral release, solo bassoon and flute, harps, organ and string-muting instructions.

transitions.title: Two voices over running flutes
transitions.from: C · Bassoon, flute and solo strings
transitions.to: D · Contralto and tenor in canon
transitions.how: The choir holds its last chord into the new 3/4 metre. At Sans lenteur, flutes rise through semiquavers while the organ’s right hand descends over a held pedal. The contralto begins very softly; the tenor enters one bar later, repeating her phrase a fifth lower.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 69–73, figure 19: 3/4, Sans lenteur, overlapping choral release and solo entries, flute and organ semiquavers.

transitions.title: Held chords give way to runs
transitions.from: D · Contralto and tenor in canon
transitions.to: E · Low voices and racing strings
transitions.how: The choir’s long chord softens before figure 22. At Allegro, bass clarinet and bassoon begin detached runs; violas and cellos join them. Tenors and basses bring in the new words above accented horn notes. The upper strings remove their mutes as the short figures spread upwards.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 81–85, figure 22: pp subito before Allegro, detached lower winds and strings, lower-voice entry, horns and removal of violin mutes.

transitions.title: The running notes fall away
transitions.from: E · Low voices and racing strings
transitions.how: Wind and string runs climb to the end of the Allegro. Figure 23 replaces them with Lent and broad choral phrases. Brass and organ sustain the harmony while double basses plunge into rapid low figures between held notes. The last pages slow further, returning to the opening’s low instruments.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 85–90: ascending runs, figure 23 Lent, sustained brass and organ, rapid double-bass figures, then De plus en plus lent and Molto rit.

source.title: Lili Boulanger, Psaume CXXX, Durand full score (1925), plate D. & F. 10543
source.locator: Printed pp. 1–4, 11–16, 37–40, 54–58, 66–74, 81–90. The score has contralto and tenor soloists, mixed choir, two harps, organ and a large orchestra including sarrusophone.

timeline.note: Low organ notes sound above a bass-drum roll and plucked cellos and double basses.
Tuba and solo cello descend together. Muted horns join their low line.
First and second violins climb into high winding phrases after the low wind solos.
The choir enters quietly in octaves. Bassoons and cellos rise beneath it over a held organ bass.
Wind runs climb above the choir while brass and low strings hold the bass.
Contralto and solo cello sing over repeated clarinet figures, harp chords and very soft divided violins.
Bassoon, flute, solo viola and solo cello take turns above running notes in harps and organ.
The contralto returns softly with celesta, harp and organ figures, held violin chords and plucked violas.
The choir takes up the contralto’s prayer, joined by brass and the full string sections.
Contralto and tenor sing in canon above rising flute figures and descending organ notes.
Small groups of singers join the solo voices, overlapping above flute, harp and organ.
Detached clarinet, bassoon and string figures drive the Allegro beneath tenors and basses.
At Lent, broad choral phrases return over brass and organ chords. Double basses plunge through rapid low figures.
The voices sing their last prayer. Organ, low winds, brass and strings make one final swell after the choir stops.

composer.epithet: At nineteen she won the Prix de Rome; before her death at twenty-four she had written songs of lost love and psalms that shake the room.
facts: Ernest and Raïssa Boulanger’s younger daughter; Nadia’s sister
Paul Vidal for composition; Georges Caussade for counterpoint; Nadia at home
First woman to win the Premier Grand Prix de Rome in composition, 1913
Songs, psalms, chamber and orchestral music; unfinished opera La Princesse Maleine
composer.background:
At the Château de Compiègne in May 1913, five young composers were shut away writing a cantata about Faust and Helen of Troy. Someone had sent champagne. Their joint letter of thanks to the composer Fernand Halphen, dated 31 May and written out by Claude Delvincourt, called them “your young colleagues imprisoned in the château to sing the loves of Faust and Helen”. Among the signatures was Lili Boulanger’s. She was nineteen, and this was her second attempt at the Prix de Rome. Illness had forced her to withdraw the previous year.

In July she became the first woman to win the Premier Grand Prix for musical composition. Thirty-one of the Académie des Beaux-Arts’ thirty-six voters supported her. Faust et Hélène gave them a tenor in love with a woman summoned from antiquity, a mezzo-soprano Helen and a baritone devil, all carried by a substantial orchestra. The compulsory text was Eugène Adenis’s adaptation of Goethe. Lili dedicated the score to Nadia, who had won a second prize in 1908.
